Seven paths, from the skin to the store in the app, that follow something of yours on a platform up to what you can demand.
Your store sells through the app. Who runs your business? · Follow the store · Lex Plataformae
Follow the store
<1>Your store sells through the app.</1> <2>Who runs your business?</2>
You run a restaurant on iFood, or sell on Mercado Livre, Shopee or Amazon. Customers arrive through the platform's screen, and it decides who appears, how much it costs to appear and who stays there.
This path follows your store, from the day you opened inside the app to the day it vanished from search, and ends with what you can demand.
<1>1</1> Whose customer is it?
The customer buys from you, but arrives through the platform. It shows your store, keeps the order history and decides whether the customer sees you again tomorrow.
Without its screen, your store is invisible. That dependence is the starting point of everything.
<1>2</1> How much does it cost to show up?
More and more. Promotions, coupons you subsidise and featured plans become a condition for showing up well. The platform decides which stores will be seen, in what order and with which badges.
Whoever controls where you appear controls, in practice, how much you sell.

It defines, or at least strongly conditions, which competitors will be visible, on what terms they will be compared, under what reputation signals they will appear, what kind of friction they will suffer, what strategic data will be extracted from their activity and how the user will perceive the very space of choice.<1>p. 771</1>
<1>3</1> And when the rule changes?
The commission rises, the cancellation policy changes and the ranking criterion is redone. It all arrives by notice, without negotiation. You stay inside, but in a worse position.
A change like that does not need to exclude you to take away the value of staying there.

Functional value equivalence, in turn, makes it possible to control rule changes that, without formally excluding certain agents, significantly lower their practical position in the ecosystem, emptying the usefulness of competitive permanence under the pretext of updating, optimisation or a change of internal policy.<1>p. 772</1>
<1>4</1> Is the rating fair?
Not always. Your rating drops because of a delivery delay you do not control, a cancellation that was not yours or a complaint you cannot challenge. And the rating defines who appears first.
You answer to a reputation system whose criteria you cannot check.
<1>5</1> Who owns the buyers' data?
The platform. It knows who buys from you, how much, when and what else they look for, and you see only part of it. This data is worth a lot, including to the platform itself.
<1>6</1> Does the platform also compete with you?
Sometimes, yes. It organises the market in which you sell and, at the same time, can sell on its own account, favour partners or sign exclusivity deals. When that happens, the referee also plays.
The variety of stores on the screen does not guarantee a real choice, neither for the customer nor for you.
<1>7</1> What can you demand when the store disappears?

You can demand the concrete reason for the suspension, a real chance of defence, the preservation of the store's records and minimum clarity about the ranking and reputation criteria. When the suspension has no verifiable reason, reinstatement can be requested.

Selling does not strip you of all protection. Consumer law can reach the merchant who depends on the platform to that degree. When it does not reach, the case proceeds under the Civil Code, and practices that distort competition can be taken to Cade, the competition authority.

In Goiás, a merchant had her iFood profile blocked without notice. The Public Defender's Office argued that the block, without notification and without a chance of defence, violated the right to be heard and interrupted an activity of more than two years. The Court of Justice recognised that the block was wrongful, with reinstatement and compensation.

At Cade, the investigation into iFood's exclusivity with restaurants ended in a 2023 settlement that banned exclusivity with chains of 30 or more outlets and set other limits. iFood was not fined, and the settlement itself treats exclusivity as lawful within those limits. The case shows the weight of whoever organises the market in which everyone sells.

You bought on a marketplace. Who chose what you bought? · Follow the order · Lex Plataformae
Follow the order
<1>You bought on a marketplace.</1> <2>Who chose what you bought?</2>

You searched for a product in an online store with many sellers, chose among the offers on the screen and paid. What arrived was not what you expected, or did not arrive, and the store replied that it only intermediates.
This path follows your order, from the search to the dispute, and ends with what you can demand.
<1>1</1> Were you seeing the market?
It seemed so. The screen showed dozens of offers, with prices, photos and stars, as if the whole market were there, side by side.
But what reached you had already gone through a selection. The store chose what appears first, what stays hidden and what seems comparable.
The consumer does not choose in a vacuum, before a transparent and symmetrical universe of offers.<1>p. 762</1>
<1>2</1> Who decided the order on the screen?

The store. The position of each offer depends on criteria it defines, and part of the shop window is sold to whoever pays for prominence. When the paid ad looks like an ordinary result, you cannot tell one from the other.
That makes the store much more than a corridor through which seller and buyer pass. It manufactures the market you see.
<1>3</1> Were the stars telling the truth?
Stars, trusted-seller badges and best-seller tags weighed on your choice. But you cannot check how those ratings are calculated, who gives them or what is left out of them.
The trust the screen conveys is also organised by the store, along with the order of the offers.
It administers criteria of presentation, trust, prioritisation and legibility of the market accessible to the consumer.<1>p. 762</1>
<1>4</1> Whom did you pay?
The store. The money went through its payment system, often the delivery too, and it keeps the record of everything that happened between the click and your front door.
That is why the store is not just a shop window where others sell. It organises the whole sale.
In both cases, the platform does not merely host listings.<1>p. 762</1>
<1>5</1> And when the order goes wrong?

The product arrives different from the photo, counterfeit or defective, or simply does not arrive. The usual answer is that the store only put you in touch with the seller and that the responsibility is his.
That answer ignores what happened before. The purchase went wrong inside an environment the store built, ordered and sold as trustworthy.
Platforms of this nature do not merely connect.<1>p. 761</1>
<1>6</1> Who decides the dispute?
The store itself. It receives your complaint, hears the seller, looks at the records only it holds and decides who is right.
